en: The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the Blessed One was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, during the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone on his alms-round through the city in due order, he returned to his place.
When he had finished eating his meal, in the afternoon, he put away his robe and bowl and washed his feet.
As was his custom, he spread his seat, sat down cross-legged, held his body erect, and established right mindfulness before him.
Then the bhikṣus all went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti was seated together with the great assembly.

Then the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, well protects and cherishes all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas because of their unsurpassed benefit;
he well entrusts all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas because of his unsurpassed teaching.
“World-Honored One!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practices the Bodhisattva vehicle, how should they dwell?”
"How should one practice?
How does one give rise to the bodhicitta?
Having asked this, the Venerable Subhūti [spoke].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Subhūti:
“Subhūti, excellent, excellent!
Thus it is, noble son!
The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of supreme benefit;
he well entrusts all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of the supreme teaching.
Subhūti! Therefore, now listen with a single-minded focus, with reverence, and reflect upon it well.
I shall now speak for you.
"Just as a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment and practices the bodhisattva vehicle, so should they abide, so should they practice,
and so should they generate the mind. Subhūti said, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “Subhūti!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta and practices the vehicle of the bodhisattva should resolve their mind in this way:”

"Whatever categories of sentient beings there may be—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—even including the entire realm of sentient beings as it is conventionally designated."
"Such sentient beings as these, I shall all establish in nirvana without remainder.
Although he thus brings immeasurable sentient beings to nirvana, not a single sentient being is actually brought to nirvana.
Why is this? Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva has the notion of a "sentient being," then he should not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti,
all bodhisattvas are without the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without attachment to their own kind, without attachment to others, and should practice giving without attachment to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena."
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, without attachment to the perception of signs. Why is that?
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment, this mass of merit is incalculable. Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Can the space in the eastern direction be measured? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, "So it is, Subhūti!"
“In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below— in the empty space of the ten directions—
can it be measured? Subhūti replied, “It cannot, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment, this mass of merit is likewise immeasurable."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the excellence of his physical marks?”
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
The excellent physical marks and virtues spoken of by the Tathāgata are not [truly] excellent marks and virtues."
"Why is this? Subhūti! All marks whatsoever are entirely false and illusory."
The absence of any marks is itself reality.
By means of the markless nature of marks, one should perceive the Tathāgata.
Having spoken thus, [he remained silent].
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,

in the present time and in future ages, will there be any bodhisattvas who, upon hearing such chapters and verses of this sutra as these descriptions are correctly explained, will conceive the thought that they are real?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus:

'In the present time and in future ages, will there be any bodhisattvas who, upon hearing such chapters and verses of this sūtra spoken in this manner, will give rise to the notion that they are real?'"
Why is this? Subhūti! In future ages, there will truly be sentient beings who, upon hearing this sutra, will be able to give rise to the perception of reality.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! In a future age, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is perishing, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who maintain the precepts, cultivate merit, and possess wisdom."

Subhūti! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not served only one buddha, nor have they planted roots of goodness under only one buddha; rather, they have already served immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddhas and have already planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddhas.

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing such passages and phrases from this sutra as these correctly explained characteristics, should give rise to even a single thought of true faith.
Subhūti! The Tathāgata fully knows these people; the Tathāgata fully sees these people. Subhūti!
These sons and daughters of good family will produce and grow an immeasurable accumulation of merit!
Why is this? Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas no longer have the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient.
These bodhisattvas have neither the notion of dharmas nor the notion of non-dharmas; they have neither notion nor non-notion.
Why is this? Subhūti,
if these bodhisattvas have the notion of a dharma, that is precisely the grasping at a self, as well as the grasping at a sentient being, a life-span, and a recipient.
Subhūti! For this reason, a bodhisattva should not grasp at dharmas, nor should they grasp at non-dharmas.
It is for this purpose that the Tathāgata has said:
"If a practitioner of the path understands the Parable of the Raft Sūtra, they should abandon even the Dharma, let alone what is non-Dharma.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma?"
Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has attained, which is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
nor is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has preached."
Why is this? This Dharma taught by the Tathāgata cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed;
it is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Why is this? Because all noble ones are manifested through the unconditioned True Suchness. "Subhūti!..."
What do you think?
If someone were to take the seven treasures filling the entire trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift, would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on account of this giving?
Subhūti said: “Very much, World-Honored One! Very much, Sugata!”
These sons and daughters of good family, by virtue of this giving, shall obtain exceedingly great merit. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
"This accumulation of merit is, in fact, not an accumulation of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as 'an accumulation of merit. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take a great trichiliocosm filled with the seven treasures and offer it as a gift;

and if there were another person who, from this sutra, were to receive even a single four-line verse and correctly explain it for others, revealing its meaning—[the latter would generate far more merit].
By this causal condition, the merit produced by this person will be far greater than that, immeasurable and incalculable.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata is accomplished through this merit.
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are born from this merit. Why is this so?
Subhūti! What is called "Buddha-dharma" is not Buddha-dharma; it is merely designated as "Buddha-dharma. Subhūti!
What do you think? Could a stream-enterer have the thought:
"I have attained the fruit of stream-entry"?
"No, World-Honored One," Subhūti replied. "It could not."
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
Because in reality there is nothing that can enter the stream, one is therefore called a *srotāpanna*.
The same applies even to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; therefore, one is called a Srotāpanna.
A Sakṛdāgāmin is so named because they "return once"; yet in reality, there is nothing that can go or return, and thus one is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
“Anāgāmin is called ‘one who does not come back. In reality, there is nothing that can reach the state of ‘not coming back’;
this is what is meant by ‘Anāgāmin. The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”
What do you think? Could an Arhat have the thought:
"I have attained the fruit of Arhatship"?
"Is this not so? Subhūti replied,
"It could not, World-Honored One!"
For what reason? Because,
World-Honored One, there is in reality nothing that can be called an arhat.
If an Arhat should have this thought: "I have attained the fruit of Arhatship," this thought is itself the grasping at a self,
the grasping at a sentient being, the grasping at a life-span, and the grasping at a recipient.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has praised me as the foremost among those who dwell in the samādhi of non-contention.
World-Honored One!
"I have now attained arhatship and am free from the desires of the three realms of existence.
World-Honored One!
I do not even harbor such thoughts as these:"
"I am an Arhat. World-Honored One! If I had such a thought:
"If I had already attained the fruit of arhatship,
the Tathāgata would not have bestowed this prediction upon me:
'Among those who dwell in the samādhi of non-contention, the son of good family Subhūti is the foremost.'"
"In truth, there is no abiding; one abides in non-contention, one abides in non-contention.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
"In the past, from the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, was there even a single dharma that the Tathāgata took up?
Subhūti replied, "He took up nothing, World-Honored One."
"In truth, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata received from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there should be a bodhisattva who speaks as follows:"
"I shall adorn and purify a Buddha-field"—
this bodhisattva speaks a false word. Why is this?
Subhūti! That which is called the adornment of Buddha-fields, the Tathāgata says is not an adornment; it is for this reason that it is called the adornment of pure Buddha-fields. Subhūti!

Therefore, a bodhisattva should give rise to such a mind that is free from dwelling and attachment; they should not give rise to a mind that dwells on forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, but should give rise to that mind by dwelling nowhere at all.
“Subhūti! Suppose there were a person whose physical form was as vast and great as Mount Sumeru. Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Is such a nature and characteristic supreme and great? Subhūti replied:
“Very great, World-Honored One! Why is this?
That which the Tathāgata calls the ‘body of existence’ is not a body of existence; it is because it is not a body of existence that it is called the ‘body of existence.’”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, would the grains of sand in all those Ganges be numerous?"
Subhūti said: “Very many, World-Honored One!
Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already countless, how much more so their sands.”
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! I now awaken you; I now reveal it to you.”

If there were as many worlds as there are grains of sand in all the Ganges Rivers, and a son or daughter of good family were to fill them entirely with the seven precious treasures and offer them as a gift to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Subhūti, what do you think? By reason of this, would that person acquire much merit?
Subhūti said: "Very many, World-Honored One! Very many, Sugata!"
"By this cause and condition, this person generates exceedingly great merit.
Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift."
If any son or daughter of good family, from this sutra down to even a single four-line verse, respectfully receives and upholds it, and correctly expounds it for others.
The merit produced by this person will be far more supreme, immeasurable, and incalculable than that!
"Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever anyone is able to read, recite,
or explain from this sutra even as little as a single four-line verse, [that place shall become a true shrine for the world]."
You should know that this place shall become a caitya within the world, which all humans, devas, asuras, and others ought to revere.
How much more so for anyone who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite such a sutra as this; you should know that such a person is in accord with the unsurpassed and most rare Dharma.
"In this place, the Great Teacher is present, or there is at least one person worthy of respect.
When the Buddha had spoken these words,
the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the title of this sutra? How shall we uphold it?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This sūtra is named 'Prajñāpāramitā. By this name, you should uphold it."
Why is this? Subhūti,
that which the Tathāgata calls the perfection of wisdom is, as the Tathāgata has taught, not a perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, what do you think? Is there even a single dharma that has been taught by a Buddha?
Subhūti said: "There is none, World-Honored One!
There is not a single dharma that a Tathāgata has taught."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Are all the atoms contained within the trichiliocosm many? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One, these minute particles of this world are exceedingly many!
Sugata, they are exceedingly many! Why is this?
"Bhagavān! These atoms, which the Tathāgata says are not atoms, are therefore called 'atoms.
These worlds, which the Tathāgata says are not worlds, are therefore called 'worlds.'"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?"
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One! Why is this so?"
"These thirty-two marks of a great man, the Tathāgata has said, are not marks; therefore they are called the 'thirty-two marks of a great man.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many times as there are grains of sand in all the Ganges Rivers, were to give up their lives and bodies in such numbers as those grains of sand as acts of giving."
If there are good sons or good daughters who, from this sutra down to even a single four-line verse, respectfully receive and uphold it, and correctly expound it for others.
"By this cause and condition, this person will produce merit far exceeding that [of the former], immeasurable and incalculable.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, moved by the swift power of the Dharma-benefit, immediately wept with grief.
Wiping away his tears, he said:
“How rare, World-Honored One! How rare, Sugata!”
Such a sūtra as this has been spoken by the Tathāgata; from the past until I attained noble wisdom, I have never before heard such a sūtra being taught. Why is this?
The World-Honored One speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet it is not [truly] the *prajñāpāramitā*; therefore it is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
You should know that such a person is endowed with the unsurpassed and most rare Dharma; when hearing this sutra being preached, they are able to give rise to the perception of reality.
World-Honored One!
This so-called "real perception" is, in truth, not a perception; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as "real perception," and speaks of it as "real perception.
World-Honored One!
"This matter is not surprising to me.
While the sutra was being correctly preached, I gave rise to faith and understanding.
World-Honored One!"

In future ages, if there are sentient beings who respectfully receive and uphold this, and correctly expound it for others, you should know that such persons will be in accord with the unsurpassed and most rare Dharma.
World-Honored One!
This person no longer has the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient. Why is this?
The notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of a recipient—these are all non-notions. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have liberated themselves from all notions without exception.
Having spoken these words,
the Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, Subhūti!”
Thus you should know that such a person is endowed with the unsurpassed and most rare Dharma.
Upon hearing this sutra being preached, such a person is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear.
Why is this? Subhūti! This Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata is the foremost pāramitā.
"This pāramitā is taught by the Tathāgata; immeasurable Buddhas have also taught it in this same way. Therefore, it is called the foremost pāramitā. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Tathāgata’s perfection of patience is not a perfection. Why is this so, Subhūti?

In the past, when I was King Kaliṅga and my body was hacked and cut apart until my flesh and bones were shattered, at that time I had no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-span, and no notion of a recipient; there was neither thought nor non-thought.
Why is this? Subhūti!

If, at that time, I had possessed the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a recipient, then at that time I would have given rise to thoughts of resentment.
Subhūti! I recall that in five hundred past lives, I was a great ṛṣi named Kṣāntivādin.
Throughout all those births, my mind was free from the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of a recipient.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should relinquish all perceptions and give rise to the mind directed toward unsurpassed awakening; they should not give rise to a mind that dwells on form, nor should they give rise to a mind that dwells on sound, odor, taste, or touch; they should not give rise to a mind that dwells on mental phenomena (*dharma*), nor should they give rise to a mind that dwells on what is not a mental phenomenon (*adharma*); they should not give rise to a mind that dwells anywhere at all.
Why is this? If the mind has a dwelling place, then it is not truly dwelling.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says:
"A Bodhisattva should practice giving with a mind that dwells nowhere.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner for the benefit of all sentient beings.
This notion of "sentient beings" is itself a non-notion.
Thus, all these sentient beings, the Tathāgata says, are themselves non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are far removed from all conceptualizations. "Subhūti!
What the Tathāgata speaks is reality, he speaks truth, he speaks suchness, and he speaks that which is not false."
Furthermore, Subhūti!
This Dharma is that which has been awakened to by the Tathāgata; this Dharma is that which has been taught by the Tathāgata; this Dharma is neither real nor unreal. "Subhūti!"
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person in total darkness; in this way, one should know that a bodhisattva who falls into signs practices giving that falls into signs.

Subhūti, it is as if a person with eyes, when the night has turned to dawn and the light of the sun shines during the day, sees various forms; in this way, one should know that a bodhisattva who does not fall into signs practices signless giving.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! In future ages, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sūtra, and correctly expound it for others, the Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they shall produce and grow an immeasurable accumulation of merit."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there are good men or good women who, during the morning portion of the day, give away their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the aforementioned rivers;

and during the midday portion of the day, they give away their bodies and lives; and during the afternoon portion of the day, they give away their bodies and lives—all as many times as the sands of the aforementioned rivers."
If one were to practice such giving of body and life for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas,

and another person were to hear this sutra and not give rise to slander, the merit produced by the latter through this cause and condition would be infinitely and immeasurably greater than that of the former.
How much more so for those who copy, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, teach others to practice it, and explain it extensively for others.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, such a sūtra as this is inconceivable; none can equal it."
The Tathāgata speaks only for the sake of compassion and benefit for those who can practice the Unsurpassed Vehicle and those who practice the Peerless Vehicle.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone in future ages who receives, maintains, reads, recites, teaches others to practice, and correctly expounds this sutra.
The Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they are endowed with an inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable mass of merit.
Such persons as these, by means of my own body, will be able to bear the burden of unsurpassed bodhi.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Regarding such a sutra as this, it is impossible for those who have inferior aspirations and desires, or those who hold views of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, or a recipient, to be able to hear, practice, read, recite, or correctly explain it to others.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Wherever this sutra is proclaimed and expounded, all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and so forth—should make offerings, prostrate, and circumambulate it to the right.
"You should know that this place shall become a caitya within the world.
Subhūti! If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, recite, teach others to practice, and correctly expound such sūtras as these,"
This person currently undergoes such things as being treated with contempt.
The evil karma created in past lives, which would otherwise have resulted in the retribution of rebirth in the evil realms, is instead exhausted by undergoing slight suffering in the present life.
Consequently, their past sins and the resulting bitter retribution are extinguished, and they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Subhūti! I recall that in the past, beyond countless, immeasurable, and incalculable great eons, after the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, there were eighty-four thousand times ten million koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who attained Buddhahood; I served, made offerings to, and honored them all, and none were left unattended.”

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be someone who, during the final five-hundred-year period of the latter age, receives, maintains, reads, recites, teaches others to practice, and correctly expounds this sutra. Subhūti!

The mass of merit produced by this person cannot be matched even by a hundredth part of the merit I obtained from serving and making offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the past; it does not reach a ten-million-billionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation, nor even by any analogy corresponding to its power or category.

“Subhūti! If I were to fully describe the merit obtained by good sons and good daughters who, in the final age at the end of time, receive, uphold, read, and recite such sūtras as these—if a good son or good daughter were to listen attentively and remember such a mass of blessings, their minds might become confused or they might even go mad.”
Furthermore, Subhūti, such a sutra as this is inconceivable; if a person practices it and attains its karmic fruit, that too is inconceivable.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a son of good family or a daughter of good family, who has resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practices the bodhisattva vehicle, abide?”
"How does one practice?
How does one give rise to the bodhisattva mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
‘I shall establish all sentient beings and cause them to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.’”
"In this way, although immeasurable sentient beings have been brought to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has been brought to nirvāṇa.
Why is that? Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva harbors the notion of a "sentient being," then he should not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti!
"In reality, there is no dharma that can be called 'one who practices the Bodhisattva's Supreme Vehicle.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
"At the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata obtained which is called 'anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
"At the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was not a single dharma that the Tathāgata obtained which could be called 'anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi'.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Subhūti!"
It is so. At the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was not a single dharma that the Tathāgata obtained which could be called *anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti!

If, at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there were even a single dharma obtained by the Tathāgata called *anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*, then the Buddha Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: "O Brahmin!..."
In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

"Subhūti! Because there is truly no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained which is called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' for this reason the Buddha Dīpaṃkara conferred upon me the prediction, saying: 'O Brahmin!'"
In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Why is this? Subhūti! "Tathāgata" is another name for True Suchness (tathatā).
“Subhūti! If someone were to say:
‘The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
"This person speaks untruthfully. Why is that? Subhūti!"
In truth, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has attained which could be called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Subhūti,
this dharma attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor unreal."
Therefore, the Tathāgata says:
"All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti!
"All dharmas," Subhūti, are so called by the Tathāgata because they are not all dharmas.
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person with a vast body, a body encompassing the whole."
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!
This 'pervasive body' and 'great body' spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, no-body; for this reason they are called the 'pervasive body' and the 'great body'."
The Buddha said: “So it is, Subhūti! So it is, Subhūti!”
If there is a bodhisattva who speaks these words:
"I shall bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then one should not call him a bodhisattva.
Subhūti, what do you think? Is there even a single dharma that is called "bodhisattva"?
Subhūti said: “There are none, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! For this reason, the Tathāgata says:
‘All dharmas are without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, and without a recipient.’”
"Subhūti! If there is a bodhisattva who speaks these words:
'I shall adorn and purify a buddha-field.'"
"A bodhisattva who speaks such words utters falsehood.
Why is this, Subhūti?"
"Adorning the Buddha-fields," the Tathāgata says, "is not adorning; therefore it is called 'adorning the pure Buddha-fields.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva has faith and perceives that all phenomena are without self, and that all phenomena are without self, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has said:"
"This is called a bodhisattva; this is called a bodhisattva. "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? Subhūti replied,
“It is so, World-Honored One.”
"The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?”
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye.”
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
Subhūti replied, “It is so, World-Honored One.”
“The Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. "Subhūti!"
What do you think?

If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and if there were as many worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would these not be very numerous?
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The number of these worlds is exceedingly great.”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Within all those worlds, I see and know all sentient beings dwelling in their continuous mental streams; they are of various kinds.”
Why is this? Subhūti, the continuity of the mind abides;
the Tathāgata says it is not a continuity that abides, and therefore he speaks of its continuity.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
If someone were to take seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm and give them as a gift, would that son or daughter of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?”
Subhūti said: “Very much, World-Honored One! Very much, Sugata!”
The Buddha said: “So it is, Subhūti! So it is.”
"By this causal condition, those sons and daughters of good family will acquire a vast accumulation of merit. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
If the heap of merit were merely a heap, then the Tathāgata would not say, "This is a heap of merit;
this is a heap of merit. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body. Why is this?"
"This perfection of the physical body, the Tathāgata says is not a perfection of the physical body; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'perfection of the physical body.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the possession of the various marks? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the various marks. Why is this?
"This mark of perfection, the Tathāgata says, is not a mark of perfection; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as a mark of perfection. The Buddha said: "Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata harbor such a thought as:
'I am now truly teaching the Dharma'?"
"Is that so, Subhūti? If someone were to say: "
"You should know that the Tathāgata truly is able to teach the Dharma;
yet this person, due to their lack of true existence and their false attachments, gives rise to slander against me."
Why is this? Subhūti,
"the teaching of the Dharma, the teaching of the Dharma"— in reality, there is no dharma that can be called the teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing the correct exposition of such characteristics as these chapters and verses of this sutra, will give rise to true faith?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"They are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings. Why is this?"
Subhūti! Those sentient beings whom the Tathāgata speaks of are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings; therefore, he speaks of them as "sentient beings. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has attained which is called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'? Subhūti replied:
“No, World-Honored One!
There is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata has attained which could be called ‘anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti! So it is.

There is not even a dharma as small as a mote of dust that has been relinquished by the Tathāgata or attained by the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'—perfectly equal and equanimous."
Furthermore, Subhūti, the awakening and realization of all Buddhas is without distinction; for this reason, it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
This Dharma is equal, without high or low; it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this Dharma is equal—due to the absence of a self of phenomena, the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a life-span, the absence of a recipient, and so forth—it is therefore called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is by means of the complete fulfillment of genuine wholesome dharmas that one attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!
As for what is called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not dharmas; therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas. "Subhūti!
Suppose there were as many heaps of the seven treasures as there are Mount Sumerus, kings of mountains, in this trichiliocosm, and someone were to take these and give them as a gift.

If a person, from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly explain even as little as a four-line verse for others, the merit they would thereby obtain would be such that the previously mentioned merit could not equal one-hundredth part of it; it could not equal one-ten-millionth, one-billionth, or even one-trillionth part of it; it would be beyond the reach of all calculation, and no analogy corresponding to its power or category could possibly equal it.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata have such a thought as this:”
"Do you think, Subhūti, that [the Tathāgata thinks], 'I have delivered sentient beings'?"
You should not now entertain such a thought.
Why is this? In reality, there are no sentient beings who are delivered by the Tathāgata.

Subhūti! If there were any sentient beings who were liberated by the Tathāgata, that would constitute grasping at a self, grasping at a sentient being, grasping at a life-span, and grasping at a recipient.
Subhūti! This grasping at a self, which the Tathāgata says is not grasping, is so called because it is the grasping of infantile, ordinary worldlings. Subhūti!
"Those who are called infantile ordinary beings, the Tathāgata says they are not beings; therefore, he speaks of 'infantile ordinary beings.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the marks? Subhūti replied,
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the marks.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti! So it is.”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the marks of physical perfection. Why is this?

If one were to perceive the Tathāgata by means of the marks of physical perfection, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would also be a Tathāgata; therefore, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the marks of physical perfection.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me by means of sound,
Such a person walks upon a deviant path And shall not be able to see me."
One should see the Buddha through the Dharma; the Dharma is the body of the Tamer.
This Dharma is not the domain of consciousness; the suchness of the Dharma is profound and difficult to perceive. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think,
Subhūti? Can a Tathāgata attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection?"
You should not now hold such a view as this:
"The Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection. Why is that?
Subhūti! The Tathāgata does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of being endowed with the marks. Subhūti!
If you should think: "The Tathāgata has said this:
'For those who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle, there is a dharma that can be extinguished.'"
"Subhūti! Do not hold such a view. Why is that?
The Tathāgata does not say that for one who practices the vehicle of the bodhisattva, there is any dharma that can be extinguished or ever severed. "Subhūti!
Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, were to offer them as a gift."

If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding all phenomena as selfless and unarisen, attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, then by virtue of these causes and conditions, the merit they obtain will be far greater than that of the former.
“Subhūti! One who practices the Great Vehicle should not grasp at the accumulation of merit. Subhūti said:
“Can this mass of merit be grasped? The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”
This accumulation of merit can be gathered and maintained, but it cannot be grasped.
Therefore, it is said that this accumulation of merit should be gathered and maintained. "Subhūti!
If someone were to say,
"The Tathāgata walks, stands, sits, or lies down," that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? Subhūti, the Tathāgata has no place to which he goes, nor any place from which he comes; for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the atoms of earth in a trichiliocosm, burn them to ashes and powder, and combine them into ink pellets as numerous as the collection of those atoms.”
Subhūti, what do you think? Is this collection of atoms great?
Subhūti said: "That collection of atoms is very great,
World-Honored One!"
Why is this? World-Honored One!
If the collection of atoms were substantially existent, then the World-Honored One would not refer to it by the name "collection of atoms."
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
This "aggregation of atoms" spoken of by the Tathāgata is, as the Tathāgata says, not an aggregation of atoms; it is for this reason that it is called an "aggregation of atoms."
The "trichiliocosm" spoken of by the Tathāgata is, in truth, not a world; therefore it is called the "trichiliocosm.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
If one clings to the world as being substantially existent, this is the clinging to a collection as a unity.
This clinging to a collection as a unity, the Tathāgata says, is not clinging; therefore, it is called "clinging to a collection as a unity."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
“Subhūti! This ‘grasping at a collection’ is merely a worldly convention.”
Subhūti! This Dharma is not a Dharma that can be expressed in words; it is grasped through the biased speech of infantile ordinary beings. Subhūti!
Subhūti, if someone were to say:
"The Tathāgata has taught the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a recipient," [they would be mistaken].
"What do you think?
Is the speech of this person correct speech? Subhūti replied:
"It is improper, Blessed One!
It is improper, Sugata! Why is that?

The views of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, and a recipient spoken of by the Tathāgata are in fact no-views; therefore, they are called the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a recipient.
“Subhūti! If a person practices the Bodhisattva vehicle, they should thus know, see, and believe all dharmas;
they should thus cultivate them so that the notion of a dharma does not arise.”
Why is this? Subhūti, as for this "conception of dharmas," the Tathāgata has said that it is not a conception; therefore, it is called the "conception of dharmas."

“Subhūti! If there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with the seven treasures filling countless and immeasurable worlds, were to offer them as a gift; and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, were to receive, uphold, read, and recite even as little as a four-line verse, and teach others to practice it and explain it extensively for them—[the latter would generate far greater merit].”
By these causes and conditions, the merit produced by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than that [of the former], immeasurable and incalculable.
How then shall this sutra be proclaimed?
Because there is nothing to be manifested in what is taught, it is called "manifest teaching.
"As suchness is immovable, there is always the correct teaching.
One should contemplate conditioned phenomena as being like darkness, cataracts, a lamp, and a magical illusion; like dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud."

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti’s heart was filled with joy and progress; likewise, the assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as humans, devas, asuras, and all other beings in the world, leaped for joy and, with faith and acceptance, put it into practice.
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Ujjayinī in Western India, named Kuṇarata, which in this language means Paramārtha.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty sent messengers from afar to welcome him. As he traveled through Min and Yue, he stayed briefly at Liang’an.

The Prefectural Governor Wang Fangshe was devoted to the True Dharma and by nature fond of the Mahāyāna; he subsequently constructed a monastery and invited [the Master] to propagate these scriptures there.
The Dharma Master did not deviate from his original vow and remained silent despite receiving three invitations.
Upon examining this old translation, he found it contained many omissions and errors.

Consequently, on the first day of the fifth month in the Renwu year, he retranslated it; the Sanskrit text was standardized according to the commentary of Vasubandhu. The Dharma Master was proficient in local dialects, so there was no need for an interpreter.
Gazing upon those profound texts, he proclaimed these abstruse expositions.
Together with Dharma Master Zong, Faqian, and others, I served as the scribe for the transcription.
On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, the text and its meaning were fully completed.
The sūtra consists of one fascicle, while its commentary comprises ten fascicles.
Faguan personally inspected them and further vowed to produce one hundred copies for circulation and offering, as well as to lecture upon them ten times.
May all sentient beings, by means of this correct teaching, swiftly attain nirvana and perpetually manifest through responsive transformations.
